name: Victor Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at Cartwheel Commerce, which runs a platform for online shops. I'm on the checkout team, so my day is connecting shops to payment and delivery services and fixing it when a parcel label prints wrong. I use AI tools all day, and I'm not shy about it. My code isn't the cleanest on the team yet, but I get things working fast.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell a small plugin I built myself that prints delivery labels in bulk for shops, and it makes about 250 a month. I live with Hana, my girlfriend, who's a physiotherapist. My dad runs a car garage across town, and I still help him with his booking system when it breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd keep doing what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and anyone who isn't using them is leaving money on the table. Online I'd post about my plugin and how I built it faster with AI. I'd also say the market sorted out the hype, which is how it should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and my side business keeps growing slowly. Nothing radical changing is actually good for a small seller like me. I just keep stacking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Cartwheel and aim to get my plugin to 500 a month by the end of next year. I'd put half of what the plugin makes into an index fund. I'd keep about four months of savings as my floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, pretty good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'keep stacking' mean for you, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small bits of income on top of each other: salary, the plugin, maybe a second plugin. My dad built his garage one customer at a time, and I like that model. No single boss can sink you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that Cartwheel itself has a bad year and cuts juniors. That happens in tech whether there's AI or not. I'd still have the plugin and Hana's income, so it wouldn't sink us.

say: Anyone not using AI tools is **leaving money** on the table.
The **market sorted out** the hype, which is how it should work.
think: My job's safe and my **side business** keeps growing slowly.
Nothing radical changing is good for a **small seller** like me.
do: Grow the label plugin to **500 a month** by end of next year.
Invest **half** the plugin income in an index fund.
Keep **four months** of savings as a floor.
S0.quote: My dad built his garage one customer at a time, and I like that model. No single boss can sink you.
fieldNote: His security rests on **stacked income**: salary, plugin and partner.
**Free-market** views shape how he reads the hype fading.
His father's **garage** is his model for building a living.

steps.text: Keep building checkout connections at Cartwheel
Grow the label plugin to 500 a month
Invest half the plugin income in an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding's on there. I'd want to be on the right side of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge opportunity for anyone willing to work, and that complaining won't change it. Online I'd share how I'm using AI to build plugins faster. At work I'd volunteer for every AI project going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Cartwheel would hire far fewer juniors and lean on seniors with AI. I'd probably keep my job because I'm the one already using the tools, but I wouldn't get the pay rises I'd hoped for. The plugin is where the upside is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to build a second plugin in the first six months, maybe one that answers shop customers' delivery questions automatically. I'd ask Cartwheel if I could move onto their AI checkout project. I'd reinvest plugin income into ads to grow it, maybe 100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's like the market opening early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your second plugin would answer customer questions. That's someone's job, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, someone in a small shop's back office. I think that's how markets work: the shop saves money, grows, and maybe hires for something else. I'd feel a bit uncomfortable saying that to the person, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, and employers who offer apprenticeships. Some government help for people who really can't, but not as a way of life. My dad would hire a lad from the church before he'd wait for a government scheme.

say: It's a **huge opportunity** for anyone willing to work.
**Complaining** won't change what's coming, and I'd share how I build plugins with AI.
think: Cartwheel would hire **fewer juniors**, and my pay rises would stall.
My **plugin** is where the upside is.
do: Build a **second plugin** that answers delivery questions within six months.
Ask to join Cartwheel's **AI checkout** project.
Spend about **100 a month** on ads for the plugins.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **excited**, like the market opening early.
S1.quote: My dad would hire a lad from the church before he'd wait for a government scheme.
fieldNote: He'd build a tool that **replaces** back-office work and admits discomfort.
His **traditional** outlook favours family and apprenticeships over state help.
Own job looks safe; the worry is **stalled pay**.

steps.text: Build a plugin that answers shop delivery questions
Use AI to write the second plugin in six months
Spend 100 a month on plugin ads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get moving and stop waiting for someone to save them. I'd say small businesses can still win if they're quick. At work I'd be the one keeping spirits up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job at Cartwheel is gone by 2028, because everything I do is on a screen. Worse, if AI can do any thinking work, anyone can build my plugin in an afternoon. The robots arriving in 2031 don't help me at all, but they mean Hana's physio work and my dad's garage have a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop investing and keep everything as cash, aiming for six months. I'd move my plugin money into building a proper booking and parts system for small garages, starting with Dad's, because I understand that world. When AGI lands I'd sell the plugins while they still have some value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit thrilled, a bit sick. Like the top of a roller coaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the plugins. Who would buy them in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bigger plugin shop collecting customers, for a year's revenue at most. It's not a fortune, maybe 3,000. But it's better than watching it go to zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on Hana or your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana, a bit, for a while, and I'd hate it. We'd talk about whether it makes sense to marry sooner, honestly, to pool everything properly. Dad would offer me work at the garage, and I'd take it.

say: People need to **get moving** and stop waiting to be saved.
**Small businesses** can still win if they're quick.
think: My job at Cartwheel is **gone by 2028**, since it's all screen work.
If AI does any thinking work, anyone can build **my plugin** in an afternoon.
do: Stop investing and hold **six months** of costs in cash.
Build a **booking and parts system** for small garages, starting with Dad's.
**Sell the plugins** when AGI lands, for maybe 3,000.
feel: **Anxious**, half thrilled and half sick, like a **roller coaster** top.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking work, anyone can build my plugin in an afternoon.
fieldNote: He sees his **side business** is as exposed as his job.
He uses the **robot gap** to pivot toward his dad's garage world.
Marriage talk comes from **pooling money**, not romance alone.

steps.text: Hold six months of costs in cash
Build a booking and parts system for Dad's garage
Sell the label plugins for about 3,000
Talk with Hana about marrying sooner to pool money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone who wants to start a business. I'd tell younger developers to build their own things on the side, not just rely on a salary. I'd keep it upbeat at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect to lose the Cartwheel job around 2030. But I'd have time to turn the garage software into a real product with paying customers. Garages are hands-on, so their owners keep earning until about 2034 and can pay for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd build the garage booking system with Dad as the test customer and sign up five other garages. I'd keep the job and the label plugin running while I do it. I'd invest any profit back into the garage product, not into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. More drive than dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five garages in year one. How would you find them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Through Dad. Every garage owner in town knows every other one. He'd ring a few mates and tell them his son built something that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the garage software when robots arrive around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question. Maybe the robots need booking too, or maybe the big companies take it all. I'd plan to sell the business around 2033 rather than wait to find out.

Younger developers should **build their own** things, not rely on a salary.

S3.quote: Every garage owner in town knows every other one.
fieldNote: He builds a business on **hands-on customers** who keep earning longer.

steps.text: Build garage booking software with Dad as first customer
Reinvest all profit into the garage product

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a full business life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best version for people who are willing to work and plan. I'd say families should help their young ones start things now. At work I'd say we should see it as a decade of building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is perfect for me. I'd get properly good at code, grow the plugins, and probably go full time on my own business around 2030. By the time AGI lands, I want to own something, not work for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Cartwheel for two or three more years to learn, using AI tools every day. I'd grow the plugins and start the garage software in the second year. Hana and I would marry around 2028 and probably buy a house in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Ten years is a long time if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your business fails in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go back to a job, if there are still jobs, and try again. I'd be in my thirties with experience. Dad's first garage went bust too, and he still talks about it as his best lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to own something. Why does that matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whoever owns the business decides what happens to it. My grandad was a factory worker and never decided anything. I'd rather be like my dad than my grandad.

say: This is the best version for people **willing to work** and plan.
Families should help their young ones **start things now**.
think: Ten years is **perfect for me**: get good, grow, go independent.
By the time AGI lands, I want to **own something**.
do: Stay at Cartwheel **two or three years** using AI tools daily.
Grow the plugins and start the **garage software** in year two.
Marry Hana around **2028** and buy a house in 2029.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years is **long** if you use it.
S4.quote: My grandad was a factory worker and never decided anything. I'd rather be like my dad than my grandad.
fieldNote: He sees **ownership** as the protection from AGI, shaped by family history.
Long warning brings **marriage and a house** firmly into plans.

steps.text: Use AI tools daily at Cartwheel for two or three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even my side business would be easy to copy. What would help is fewer rules and lower costs for starting a small business, plus cheap loans for people building something real. I don't want a handout, I want a fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel guilty. I would a bit, building tools that replace someone's job. But I'd rather build the tool than be the one it replaces.

headlineQuote: I'd rather build the tool than be the one it replaces.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** junior checkout developer at Cartwheel Commerce, an online shop platform.
He uses **AI tools daily** and sells a delivery-label plugin for about 250 a month.
His **traditional, free-market** views favour family, ownership and hard work over state help.
His dad's **car garage** is both his model and his next business idea.
He stays **calm to anxious**, never alarmed, because he plans to own something.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even his side business would be easy to **copy**.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** and lower costs for starting a small business.
**Cheap loans** for people building something real, not handouts.
